title: Small jobs with Lambda
bridge: A Lambda function is like a serverless API route that a cron job calls. You upload a handler and AWS runs it on a schedule. Except nothing stays in memory between calls, and each call has only the permissions of its execution role. So the role is the whole security story.
intro: Throw-away VMs must really be thrown away, even when the orchestrator is down or a run crashed. A small Python Lambda checks every 15 minutes and removes what no live run owns. It works only from tags, so it needs nothing from Temporal.

picture.caption: A schedule calls the sweeper; it reads tags, and its role lets it touch only what carries our tag.

steps.text: lists managed VMs and available disks, and reads their tags
every terminate or delete is checked against the role's tag condition
allowed only for resources tagged ai-agents:managed=true
prints what it did and why, dry_run true at first
counts orphans and deleted volumes for the alerts

p: The platform is TypeScript, but this Lambda is Python. The infrastructure repo builds its Lambdas in Python with uv, and DevOps owns them. G3-22 copies the existing modules/aws-vm-autostop, which already stops dev VMs on a schedule.

You can read it with TypeScript eyes. def is a function, indentation is the block, and a dict is an object. A list comprehension [x for x in xs] is a map. boto3 is the AWS SDK for Python: boto3.client("ec2") is like new EC2Client({}). p10-1 teaches Python properly later.

callout.text: Read type hints like TypeScript types: def parse(value: str | None) -> dt.datetime means a function from string-or-None to a datetime. Python does not check them at run time.

sections.h: The handler and its four rules
p: A Lambda function is code that AWS runs when something calls it. The entry point is the handler: here handler(event, context). Code outside it, such as creating the boto3 clients, runs once per cold start. That is the first call after AWS starts a fresh copy; later calls reuse it.
The handler looks only at VMs tagged ai-agents:managed=true and applies four rules from G3-22.

A claimed VM whose lease has passed: terminate. A VM stopped for over 72 hours: terminate, since checkpoints already saved its work. A warm-pool VM older than 24 hours: recycle, so the pool refills from the newest image. A disk that belongs to no VM: delete.
sections.because: We decide from tags alone because the sweeper must work exactly when the orchestrator is broken.

notes.text: Two AWS clients, made once per cold start. The region comes from the Lambda environment.
Dry run unless DRY_RUN is the string 'false'. Environment values are always strings.
AWS calls this with the schedule's event. We do not need it or the context.
Turns the tag list [{Key, Value}] into a dict, like Object.fromEntries.
Rule 1: a claimed VM (it has a run-id) whose lease is in the past. No live run renews it.
Rule 3: the ASG adds this tag to its own VMs. Older than 24 h means an old image.
Rule 4: 'available' means attached to nothing.

p: The helpers keep the handler short. managed_instances and managed_volumes page through results, since one call returns at most a page. parse reads the lease tag; a missing tag counts as expired.

EC2 has no 'stopped at' field. The time hides in StateTransitionReason, a text like 'User initiated (2026-10-10 08:00:00 GMT)'. If the text has no time, we return now, so the VM looks freshly stopped and is never terminated on a guess.
sections.because: We fail safe on unknown times because terminating a parked VM by mistake loses a person's place in a conversation.

notes.text: A paginator follows NextToken for us, like an async iterator over pages.
Two filters: our tag, and the states we care about.
A nested list comprehension: every instance of every reservation of every page.
No lease tag at all: treat it as expired, the oldest possible time.
A regular expression pulls the date out of the reason text.
Unknown: return now, so the 72-hour rule cannot fire.

sections.h: act(): log first, dry run at first
p: act prints one JSON line for every decision, then acts unless DRY_RUN is on. Lambda sends stdout to CloudWatch Logs, so each line is searchable later. G3-22 starts with dry_run true, like dev-vm-autostop: read a few days of lines, then switch it off.
recycle uses the Auto Scaling call with ShouldDecrementDesiredCapacity=False. The group sees a VM gone and launches a new one from the current template, which reads the newest image ID (p3-3).
sections.because: We log before we act because a cleanup job that deletes silently is impossible to trust or debug.

notes.text: One JSON line per action: what, which resource, why, and whether it was real.
In dry run we stop here: decisions are visible, nothing changes.
Terminate inside the group without lowering its count, so the pool refills.
Only reached for 'delete-volume'.

sections.h: A role that can touch only our tags
p: A Lambda runs as its execution role. G3-22 lets that role terminate VMs and delete volumes only when the resource carries ai-agents:managed=true, and recycle only in the sandbox groups. Describe calls cannot be limited by resource, so they take '*'.
If a bug made the code pick a VM without our tag, AWS would refuse the call. The role is the wall; the code is the guidance.
sections.because: We put the tag check in IAM as well as in code, because code has bugs and a deploy cannot change IAM.

notes.text: Reading is harmless and has no resource-level control.
The two destructive actions...
...only on resources whose tag says they are ours.
Recycling only inside the sandbox groups.
Writing its log lines and the metrics. Narrow the log resource to its log group in the module.

p: An EventBridge rule with the schedule rate(15 minutes) calls the function. The function is not attached to the VPC, so it needs no endpoints; it calls the EC2 API like any client.

A live run keeps its VM safe with the lease tag. workInSandbox renews ai-agents:lease-until every 5 minutes, two hours ahead (G3-20). A parked VM gets now + 73 hours. If the orchestrator dies, leases stop moving and the sweeper cleans up within 15 minutes of expiry.

G3-22 also publishes CloudWatch metrics in the namespace AIAgents/Sweeper: OrphansTerminated and VolumesDeleted. G3-34 alerts on them: a sudden rise in orphans means runs are dying without releasing their VMs.
sections.because: We wire the schedule with three CLI calls here so the Terraform in the module reads as the same three things.

code.file: the schedule's shape (the module does this in Terraform)
code.text:
aws events put-rule --name ai-agents-sandbox-sweeper --schedule-expression "rate(15 minutes)"
aws lambda add-permission --function-name ai-agents-sandbox-sweeper --statement-id every-15-minutes \
  --action lambda:InvokeFunction --principal events.amazonaws.com --source-arn "$RULE_ARN"
aws events put-targets --rule ai-agents-sandbox-sweeper --targets "Id=sweeper,Arn=$FUNCTION_ARN"

notes.text: The rule: a timer, no event pattern. 'rate(15 minutes)' is EventBridge's syntax.
The function's own policy: EventBridge, from this rule only, may invoke it.
The target: what the rule calls when it fires.

sections.h: Test it without AWS: the fixture
p: moto also works inside Python, with no server. mock_aws() swaps every boto3 call for an in-memory AWS while the block runs. A pytest fixture is like a beforeEach that hands a value to the test.
One trap: handler.py creates its clients when it is imported. So the fixture imports and reloads it inside mock_aws, after setting the region and DRY_RUN.
sections.because: We test against moto because a cleanup job is exactly the code you cannot try out on the real account.

code.text:
import datetime as dt
import importlib

import boto3
import pytest
from moto import mock_aws

PAST = (dt.datetime.now(dt.UTC) - dt.timedelta(minutes=5)).isoformat()
FUTURE = (dt.datetime.now(dt.UTC) + dt.timedelta(hours=2)).isoformat()


@pytest.fixture
def aws(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setenv("AWS_DEFAULT_REGION", "us-east-1")
    monkeypatch.setenv("DRY_RUN", "false")
    with mock_aws():
        import handler
        importlib.reload(handler)  # build its boto3 clients inside the fake AWS
        yield boto3.client("ec2"), handler


def launch(ec2, tags: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    spec = [{"ResourceType": "instance", "Tags": [{"Key": k, "Value": v} for k, v in tags.items()]}]
    reply = ec2.run_instances(ImageId="ami-03cf127a", MinCount=1, MaxCount=1, TagSpecifications=spec)
    return reply["Instances"][0]["InstanceId"]

notes.text: A lease five minutes in the past, and one two hours ahead.
A fixture: pytest calls it and passes what it yields to each test that names it.
Dry run off, so we can see real terminations.
Inside this block every boto3 call goes to moto's in-memory AWS.
Reload, so the module-level clients are created inside the fake.
Starts one VM with the given tags and returns its ID.

sections.h: Test it without AWS: the case
p: The test starts three VMs. One is an orphan with an old lease, one a live run with a fresh lease, one a stranger without our tag. After one sweep, only the orphan is gone.
The stranger matters most. It proves the sweeper ignores anything that is not ours, even with an expired lease.
sections.because: We assert on what must survive too, because a sweeper's worst bug is deleting the wrong thing.

code.text:
def state(ec2, instance_id: str) -> str:
    return ec2.describe_instances(InstanceIds=[instance_id])["Reservations"][0]["Instances"][0]["State"]["Name"]


def test_expired_lease_is_terminated_and_live_run_is_kept(aws):
    ec2, handler = aws
    orphan = launch(ec2, {"ai-agents:managed": "true", "ai-agents:run-id": "run-1", "ai-agents:lease-until": PAST})
    live = launch(ec2, {"ai-agents:managed": "true", "ai-agents:run-id": "run-2", "ai-agents:lease-until": FUTURE})
    stranger = launch(ec2, {"ai-agents:run-id": "run-3", "ai-agents:lease-until": PAST})  # not managed: not ours

    handler.handler({}, None)

    assert state(ec2, orphan) == "terminated"
    assert state(ec2, live) == "running"
    assert state(ec2, stranger) == "running"

notes.text: Reads one VM's state: running, stopped or terminated.
Ours, with a lease five minutes in the past.
Not ours: no ai-agents:managed tag.
One sweep, exactly as the schedule would call it.
The stranger survives, expired lease or not.

quiz.q: Why does the sweeper decide from tags, not by asking Temporal which runs are alive?

options.text: Lambda cannot make HTTP calls to services on inf
options.why: It could, with networking set up. The reason is independence.

options.text: So it still cleans up when the orchestrator is down or a run crashed
options.why: Tags and leases live on the VM; they need nothing else to be working.

options.text: Temporal has no API to list running workflows
options.why: It has one. We avoid depending on it on purpose.

quiz.q: Why does recycling a warm VM use ShouldDecrementDesiredCapacity=False?

options.text: Warm pools refuse calls that decrement
options.why: Decrementing is allowed; it would shrink the count.

options.text: So the VM is stopped instead of terminated
options.why: The call terminates the VM either way.

options.text: The group launches a replacement from the current template and newest image, so the pool keeps its size
options.why: That is how the pool tracks the newest image within a day.

quiz.q: The role allows ec2:TerminateInstances only with aws:ResourceTag/ai-agents:managed=true. A bug makes the code terminate an untagged VM. What happens?

options.text: AWS refuses the call; the role is the wall, not the code
options.why: The condition is checked by IAM on every call, whatever the code believes.

options.text: The VM is terminated; conditions are only logged
options.why: IAM conditions are enforced, not advisory.

options.text: Lambda retries the call until it succeeds
options.why: An AccessDenied is not retried into success.

recall: From p3-4: which tags does a claimed VM get, and what renews the lease?
From p3-1: what is the difference between a role's trust policy and its permission policy?

words.plain: Code AWS runs when something calls it, with no server to manage; do not count on memory between calls.
The function AWS calls, here handler(event, context).
A rule such as rate(15 minutes) that invokes a target on a timer.
The IAM role a Lambda runs as; its policies are all the function may do.
Log every decision but change nothing; how a cleanup job starts.
ai-agents:lease-until, a time a live run keeps pushing forward; past it, the VM is fair game.
A Python library and server that fakes AWS in memory, for tests and labs.

tickets.why: The sweeper Lambda: four tag rules, dry run first, a tag-scoped role, metrics AIAgents/Sweeper.
Alerts read the sweeper's metrics: a rise in orphans means runs die without releasing VMs.

remember: The sweeper trusts only tags: an expired lease, too old, or no owner means gone, and its role can touch nothing else.
